column3: The same superlative frame joins wholehearted submission to God with doing good, closely defining the Muslim identity claimed by the focus.
Its reversal of friendship into enmity supplies a consequence that the focus passage answers through better speech and conduct.
Repentance becomes real through righteous action directed to God, supporting the focus's union of speech and enacted reform.
It makes repentance, belief, and righteous work the path to success, a close but more general counterpart to the focus.
The immediate continuation identifies patience as the condition for receiving the better response that follows the focus's exemplary speech.
A forced claim of surrender while denying evil contrasts with the focus's credible Muslim declaration, which is joined to righteous action.
Its rhetorical question about what is better clarifies the focus's superlative form as an affirmation of God-centered excellence.
It turns God-conscious speech into repairing relations and obedience, giving a communal application of the focus's righteous action.
The belated wish to do righteousness shows why the focus's call must be authenticated by action while action remains possible.
It values belief and righteous work over worldly display and repeats the patience motif developed immediately after the focus.
The preceding verse specifies better conduct as overcoming hostility, supplying the social practice of the focus's better speech.
It links believers' righteous works to a good reward but adds little beyond the focus's action requirement.
The parallel question asserts that God's judgment is unsurpassed, but it does not directly describe the caller's speech.
Its separation-with-sufficiency theme only indirectly touches the reconciled relation in the focus's local context.
It defines submission as accepting judgment without inward resistance, deepening what it means to say one is among the Muslims.
The command to be first among the Muslims provides a prophetic model for the focus's public identity statement.
The nearby description of warning and glad tidings frames the focus's God-directed calling as proclamation that many may refuse.
It contrasts obedience with turning away and links submission to a good reward, though its call is set in a conflict scene.
A messenger's clear recitation brings believing righteous actors from darkness to light, closely modeling the focus's call joined to deeds.
The universal command to fear God supplies broad theological grounding but adds little to the focus's speech-and-action pattern.
Righteous deeds receive the best recompense, a general result already represented by earlier action-focused candidates.
Repentance, belief, and righteous work lead to the Garden, but it is redundant with earlier formulations of the same sequence.
Its declaration that God is Lord is followed by steadfastness and reassurance, directly supporting the focus's claimed identity lived consistently.
It separates the caller's work from the rejecters' work, clarifying responsibility when a God-directed message is refused.
It explicitly combines repentance, righteous work, and the declaration of being among the Muslims in a sustained life of gratitude.
It identifies beneficial speech as urging charity, recognized good, and reconciliation, a concrete social form of the focus's better speech.
Calling on God in distress then forgetting Him exposes a call not carried forward into conduct, the inverse of the focus's integrity.
Divine reassurance to Moses and Aaron does not materially clarify the focus's call, righteous action, or Muslim identity.
The nearby warning that deeds cannot be hidden reinforces accountability, but it does not develop the focus's positive pattern.
The summons to an alarming event contrasts the focus's invitational call with an unavoidable eschatological gathering.
The messenger remains a Muslim without seeking payment despite rejection, offering a close model of disinterested public calling.
Its promise to believers who do righteousness is broad and contributes little beyond prior action-and-reward candidates.
It makes the quality of deeds, not merely their quantity, the test of life and death, directly sharpening the focus's "best" speech and righteous work.
The single household of Muslims supplies only a minimal communal instance of the identity stated in the focus.
The nearby fire-versus-security contrast gives an outcome horizon but does not explain the focus's exemplary speech.
Its compelled surrender is a useful contrast to the voluntary Muslim identity in the focus, but the setting is otherwise distant.
The straight, God-given path supplies the direction toward which the focus calls, though without its speech-and-action structure.
Reconciliation, goodness, and God-consciousness show how righteous action can repair a threatened relationship in the focus's local ethical horizon.
The paired submission of Abraham and his son shows that surrender is enacted bodily and jointly, not merely declared.
It distinguishes Muslims from criminals, reinforcing that the focus's identity claim entails a morally distinct condition.
The nearby command to drown out the Quran names a direct obstacle to the hearing required for the focus's call.
The greeting of peace honors Abraham but adds little to the focus beyond the broader context of faithful submission.
Repentance, belief, and righteous work transform prior evil into good, showing the restorative force of conduct that accompanies a Godward turn.
Its general appeal to attentive hearing lacks a specific link to the focus's calling, action, or Muslim declaration.
The condemned person's wish for another chance to become a doer of good contrasts with the timely righteousness required by the focus.
A divine word of peace illustrates speech that effects a good condition, but it is not a human call to God.
The nearby arrogant claim of strength is a contrast to humble God-directed speech, but it contributes only indirectly.
The reciprocity of excellence and reward touches the focus's superlative language without clarifying its call or action.
Calling to Islam while people fabricate lies provides a direct negative counterpart to the focus's truthful God-directed invitation.
Its restraint before God and the Messenger supports reverent conduct but does not add a clear account of the focus's call.
It joins belief and righteous work with a good response and gentle speech, a partial parallel to the focus's integrated pattern.
Calling beings other than God is depicted as the most misguided and unanswered appeal, directly contrasting the focus's call to God.
The nearby rebuke of associating partners identifies the theological error opposed by the focus's God-directed call.
The hypocrites' harmful speech and fruitless deeds offer a distant negative contrast to speech verified by righteous action.
Joseph's account of divine goodness and family reunion does not specifically clarify the focus's public call or identity statement.
Its account of destroyed towns and expulsion is unrelated to the focus's speech, calling, and righteous action.
The greeting of peace to Moses and Aaron does not add to the focus's central pattern.
The prophetic command to worship God alone with warning and glad tidings supplies a direct, though general, model of God-centered proclamation.
The nearby judgment scene and rejection of partners provide background but do not materially develop the focus's positive call.
The description of good and beautiful companions has no useful connection to the focus's speech or conduct.
Abraham's dissociation from false worship gives a declarative monotheistic precedent but lacks the focus's righteous-action element.
Knowing God and seeking forgiveness offer broad devotional content, not a clear account of calling others through exemplary speech.
The repeated word of peace highlights benign speech but is too detached from the focus's call and action.
The description of a weighty word does not clarify what makes the focus's speech best.
The detailed Arabic Quran is the immediate medium of the focus's call, but the verse adds little about the caller's conduct.
Those called to prostration while able refuse, showing the grave consequence of not answering a divine summons in time.
Exclusive worship of God gives the core content toward which the focus calls, although it lacks the focus's ethical pattern.
Its description of despair before rain does not illuminate the focus ayah.
The disciples pair belief with their declaration of being Muslims, providing a responsive communal analogue to the focus's identity claim.
Its condemnation of falsehood about God is too general to add beyond the earlier contrast candidate.
The same-surah proclamation of one God, steadfast direction toward Him, and forgiveness is a direct thematic counterpart to the focus's call.
Belief and righteous works leading to Paradise are a broad, redundant consequence of the focus's action requirement.
Abraham's stated journey toward his Lord gives a concise model of deliberate Godward orientation.
The immediate continuation directs refuge in God against satanic provocation, preserving the better response demanded by the focus passage.
The greeting of peace to Elijah adds no material clarification of the focus.
Zechariah's personal prayer shows calling upon God, not the focus's call of others to God.
The warning that association nullifies deeds marks the doctrinal boundary required for righteous action to remain aligned with God.
It explicitly commands God-conscious believers to speak straight words, directly sharpening the ethical quality of the focus's best speech.
The final greeting of peace for patience is a distant result rather than an explanation of the focus's call and action.
A person calls God sincerely in harm then associates partners in ease, contrasting unstable invocation with the focus's faithful alignment.
Worldly goodness and later righteousness offer a general positive result but not the focus's speech-and-call relation.
The human question to the earth does not illuminate the focus's exemplary God-directed speech.
The nearby promise to believers who do righteous works reinforces the action element of the focus within the same surah.
Its command to fear God and speak upright words directly parallels the focus's concern with ethically sound speech.
It integrates faith, righteous action, mutual truth-speaking, and patience, strongly paralleling the focus's speech authenticated through conduct.
Its condition for useful intercession and approved speech does not explain the focus's call or righteous action.
The command to be among the first Muslims and reject rival protectors gives a close identity-and-allegiance counterpart to the focus.
Being driven into Hell has no useful explanatory connection to the focus ayah.
The general greeting of peace to messengers adds no material clarification after earlier peace formulas.
Turning from signs and refusing a call to guidance gives a direct negative counterpart to the focus's invitation to God.
The king's recognition of Joseph's trustworthiness does not clarify the focus's call, action, or Muslim identity.
A greeting of peace amid Abraham's fear is too remote from the focus's central pattern.
Night glorification after prostration does not materially clarify the focus ayah.
Those who excel receive the best and more, supporting the focus's superlative ethic but not its public call.
The contrast between injustice and the few who believe and act righteously supports the focus's demand for conduct alongside speech.
God answers the caller and commands reciprocal response and belief, illuminating the relational structure of calling toward God.
Its brief statement about those who turn away and corrupt does not add enough to the focus.
Giving the correct answer about God without proceeding to remembrance shows that correct speech alone is insufficient.
Sincere calling on God amid danger provides a vivid God-directed invocation, though its later durability is not shown here.
After a prayer is answered, steadfastness remains required, showing that God-directed speech must continue in disciplined conduct.
It pairs public invitation to submission with the messenger's duty to convey, closely framing the focus's self-identification and call to God.
It commands a community to invite to good, enjoin what is recognized, and restrain wrong, a central communal form of the focus's calling.
The best community is defined by enjoining good, forbidding wrong, and believing in God, supplying the collective ethical horizon of the focus.
The command to convey what has been revealed identifies public delivery of God's message as an indispensable prophetic responsibility.
The Quran's revelation so that its hearers may be warned gives the focus's God-directed speech its scriptural warning function.
The messenger enjoins what is right, forbids wrong, and directs people through revelation, closely joining proclamation with moral repair.
Believing men and women mutually enjoin good and forbid wrong, extending the focus's righteous calling into reciprocal community practice.
The prophet explicitly calls to God with clear insight alongside his followers, one of the closest formulations of the focus's central act.
Every community receives a messenger calling for worship of God and rejection of false powers, giving the focus a recurring prophetic pattern.
It commands invitation to God's way with wisdom, good instruction, and the best manner of argument, directly specifying excellent God-directed speech.
Believers are commanded to say what is best, directly clarifying the ethical quality named by the focus's superlative speech.
Moses and Aaron are told to speak gently to Pharaoh, providing a concrete discipline of persuasive speech under severe opposition.
Every messenger is given the same revelation to worship God alone, providing the shared core content of the focus's call.
The prophet is told to call to his Lord and not let disputants divert him, binding proclamation to steadfast direction.
It directly states that the messenger calls people to a straight path, a concise counterpart to the focus's invitation toward God.
The servants of the Merciful respond to ignorance with words of peace, illustrating conduct and speech that resist escalation.
The command to warn one's nearest relatives shows how divine proclamation begins within concrete human relationships.
The prophet is commanded to call to his Lord and reject association, directly combining invitation with exclusive devotion to God.
It requires the best mode of discourse and concludes with shared submission to one God, closely joining excellent speech and Muslim identity.
It combines prayer, enjoining good, forbidding wrong, and patience, supplying a practical discipline for the focus's righteous caller.
The prophet is named a witness, bearer of good news, and warner, directly locating the focus's calling within prophetic proclamation.
The prophet is explicitly described as a caller to God by His permission, the closest direct parallel to the focus's defining clause.
The universal sending of the messenger as bearer of good news and warner broadens the audience of the focus's God-directed call.
A man urges his people to follow the messengers, showing courageous public advocacy for revealed guidance.
Those who avoid false worship and turn to God receive good news, supplying the responsive movement expected from the focus's call.
The believing man contrasts his call to salvation with the opposing call to the Fire, making the direction and stakes of calling explicit.
It commands the prophet to invite, remain upright, and refuse to follow desires, tightly joining proclamation with steadfast conduct.
Jesus calls people to worship God as their Lord and follow a straight path, a direct monotheistic proclamation parallel.
The jinn urge their people to answer God's caller and believe, depicting the intended receptive response to the focus's invitation.
Refusing to answer God's caller carries consequence, completing the response horizon of the preceding direct call.
Jesus announces a messenger after him, providing a prophetic example of public truthful proclamation.
The messenger recites God's verses, purifies, and teaches, showing proclamation ordered toward transformed conduct.
Noah states that he called his people night and day, an emphatic model of persistent public calling to God.
Noah's public and private invitations show that God-directed calling can be sustained across different settings.
The prophet declares that he calls only upon his Lord and associates none with Him, closely matching the focus's God-centered allegiance.
The command to arise and warn gives a compact imperative form of the public calling embodied in the focus.
The command to remind establishes the messenger's role as a communicator rather than a controller of response.
